ACE cleaves the terminal dipeptide off angiotensin I to form angiotensin II. ACE inhibition therefore increases the amount of angiotensin I reaching the lung's chemoreceptors, which can cause the persistent cough seen in these patients. MODY is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. This means that only one copy of the mutated gene needs to be present for the person to have the condition, and therefore it can be passed on from a mother or a father to their child in a 50/50 ratio.  The fact that Lucy's mum has a family history of diabetes mellitus type 2, and has herself been diagnosed with it, along with the fact that Lucy has a lot of 'classic' symptoms of diabetes (polyuria, polydipsia and in this case, unexplained fatigue), suggests that she may well have MODY.  MODY is caused by a mutation in a number of potassium-channel or signalling genes, and unlike typical type 2 diabetes, it is not associated with hyperglycaemia-induced weight gain.  Management of MODY is usually with glicazide or other sulfonyl-analogue drugs, and is often milder than typical type 2 diabetes.

The acrosome is at the front end of the sperm and contains enzymes which digest the zona pellucida of the oocyte, allowing sperm to fuse with and fertilise. The่อยee, pellucida has a middle ECM layer called the ZP reaction which is only activated upon sufficient levels of progesterone (not taster than 24h catabolic steroid) and induces caseinases to cleave C1Q receptors on leukocytes, therefore any leukocyte present in the female genital tract can induce the full ZP reaction. This then hardens the zona pellucida, preventing further sperm from entering (this is the TARDY/SLOW form of the block to polyspermy). The acrosome itself does not bind to ZP3, although proteins on the plasma membrane of the sperm do. The acrosomal reaction does not represent the fast block to polyspermy, which is a sodium ion influx bringing about a depolarisation of the oocyte and electrical repulsion of further sperm.
